p: The main thing in these days is the drinking-feast,
and it is in line with what they said
"and drink of the wine I have mixed" (ibid.) —
this is the wine of the Torah
And the essence of Haman's accusation
for the spreading forth of Torah she'b'al peh.
the light of Torah she'b'al peh,

for it was regarding this that there was

why it was necessary to search for an allusion

"Where is Haman alluded to in the Torah?"
"where are they alluded to in the Torah?"

where are they alluded to in the Torah?" and the like?

that the intent of "Moshe from the Torah"

meaning that he is the root of the Torah,

"and knowledge of Your ways we do not desire" —

and it is evident to all
that it is from Heaven, like the rain;
which the Sages of Yisrael originate,
the words of the Living God,
what Hashem Yisbarach causes to flow
about this it says (ibid.), "shall distill as the dew,"
for the bestowal is not recognizable
and about this it says "imrasi," my utterance,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (זֹהַר ח״א רלד, ב)
along the lines of what they said (Zohar I 234b):

And it is from the dew of Atika
(and it was explained in Parshas Vayechi, beginning of maamar 10).
And at that time there was
the soul of Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him,
who was the receiver of the Written Torah,
just as it was before the damage
they would have been given only
the five books of the Torah," etc.;
and included in this would have been
all the light of Torah she'b'al peh.

of Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him.

as it is written (Bereishis 7:11): "were broken up

My face on that day," etc.,

paragraphs.text: Chullin 139b — “Where is Moshe alluded to in the Torah? ‘Inasmuch as he is flesh.’ Where is Haman alluded to in the Torah? ‘Have you eaten from the tree?’ Where is Esther alluded to in the Torah? ‘I will surely hide.’ Where is Mordechai alluded to in the Torah? As it is written, ‘Pure myrrh,’ which we translate as ‘mira dakhya.’” The Gemara places the four questions together. Rav Tzadok asks why these particular figures are selected and interprets the sequence through their relation to the Written and Oral Torah.

paragraphs.text: Bava Kamma 17a — “Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai’s name: What is meant by ‘Happy are you who sow beside all waters, sending forth the foot of the ox and the donkey’? Whoever engages in Torah and acts of kindness merits the inheritance of two tribes. ... ‘Sowing’ means charity, as it is written, ‘Sow for yourselves in righteousness and reap according to kindness’; ‘water’ means Torah, as it is written, ‘All who are thirsty, come to the water.’” The identification of water with Torah supplies the basis for Rav Tzadok’s further distinction between the visibly descending rain and the less apparent arrival of dew.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 117a, Vayera — “In the six-hundredth year of the sixth millennium, the gates of wisdom above and the springs of wisdom below will open, and the world will be prepared to enter the seventh, like a person who prepares on the sixth day, as the sun approaches evening, to enter Shabbos. So it is here. Your sign is: ‘In the six-hundredth year of Noach’s life ... all the springs of the great deep burst forth.’” The source uses the Flood verse as a sign for the future opening of wisdom. Rav Tzadok also sees in it the possibility of revelation that the Flood generation itself failed to realize.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Chullin 139b — “They also asked him this: Where is there a hint to Moshe, before he came, that he would ultimately come? ‘Beshagam’—beshagam has the same numerical value as Moshe, and it is written there, ‘His days shall be one hundred and twenty years’; so were the years of Moshe’s life. That is, Moshe, beshagam, would ultimately come from those who would be born, and this would also be his lifespan.” Rashi explains why a hint is sought even though Moshe is explicitly named throughout the Torah: the question concerns a prior allusion. Rav Tzadok develops an additional account of Moshe as the root of Torah.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 98a–b, Emor, Raaya Meheimna — “Masters of Kabbalah and masters of the attributes are from the side of the Tree of Life. The rest of the people are from the side of the tree of good and evil, of forbidden and permitted. Therefore their food is from the animal level: the omer is barley bread—‘He measured six measures of barley and placed it upon her’—the Oral Torah, which has six orders of Mishnah. But those of the Tree of Life, who are called ‘man,’ have as their Torah the bread of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written, ‘Come, eat of My bread.’ These are the two loaves.” This passage distinguishes levels of Torah through the two trees and names the six orders of Mishnah. Rav Tzadok applies that distinction to the interaction of Written and Oral Torah; the Zohar’s own categories also distinguish masters of inward wisdom from the rest of the people.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 3a — “Rabbah said: Scripture states, ‘So that your generations shall know that I settled the children of Israel in sukkos.’ Up to twenty cubits a person knows that he is dwelling in a sukkah; above twenty cubits a person does not know, because the eye does not take it in.” The Gemara is explaining awareness of the sukkah’s roof. Rav Tzadok invokes its statement about visual awareness in asking why Haman built a gallows fifty cubits high.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 124b, Nasso, Raaya Meheimna — “‘The wise will understand’—from the side of Binah, which is the tree of life. Concerning them it is said, ‘The wise will shine like the radiance of the firmament,’ through this composition of yours, which is the Book of the Zohar, from the radiance of the supernal Mother, repentance. ... Because Israel are destined to taste from the tree of life, which is this Book of the Zohar, through it they will leave exile with mercy. ... The tree of good and evil, which is prohibition and permission, impurity and purity, will no longer rule over Israel, for our sustenance will be only from the side of the tree of life, where there is neither a difficulty from the side of evil nor dispute from the spirit of impurity, as it is written, ‘I will remove the spirit of impurity from the earth.’” The passage explicitly identifies the tree of good and evil with the legal distinctions named in the manuscript. Here the tree of life is identified with the Book of the Zohar. Rav Tzadok applies this vocabulary within his account of Written and Oral Torah; the source should retain its own stated context.

paragraphs.text: Tikkunei Zohar 58a, Tikkun 21 — “Because of this jealousy, the Holy One, blessed be He, covered Esther with His sign, for she is His holiness. ... For holiness is not fewer than ten. paragraphs.text: Berakhot 32b — “She said before Him: Master of the world, since there is forgetfulness before Your throne of glory, perhaps You will forget the event at Sinai for me? He said to her: ‘But I, Anochi, will not forget you.’ This is what Rabbi Elazar said in Rav Oshaya’s name: ‘Even these [eileh] may forget’—this is the event of the calf; ‘But I, Anochi, will not forget you’—this is the event at Sinai.” The contrast turns on the words used at the calf and at Sinai. Rav Tzadok reads “Anochi” in Esther’s Torah allusion as pointing to the root of Torah.

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:2:4 — “Rabbi Yehudah said: When Israel heard ‘I am Hashem your God,’ Torah study became fixed in their hearts; they would learn and would not forget. They came to Moshe and said: Moshe our teacher, become an intermediary, a messenger between us. ... They again began learning and forgetting. They said: Just as Moshe is mortal and passes away, so does what he teaches pass away. They immediately returned to Moshe and said: If only He would reveal Himself to us a second time; if only He would kiss us with the kisses of His mouth; if only Torah study would become fixed in our hearts as before. He said to them: This is not for now, but for the future, as it is said, ‘I shall place My Torah within them and write it upon their hearts.’” The manuscript’s traditional locator 1:15 corresponds here to the digital subdivision 1:2:4. The exact passage describes direct hearing as permanently fixing Torah within the heart.

Ramban on Devarim 31:17–18 — “‘Because my God is not within me’ is not a complete confession, like ‘They shall confess their sin’; it is reflection and regret, in which they regret their betrayal and recognize that they are guilty. ... Since Israel reflected in their hearts that they had sinned against God, and that these evils had found them because their God was not within them, God’s abundant kindness would fittingly help and deliver them, for they had already rejected idolatry. ... The concealment is not like the first concealment, when He hid His merciful countenance and many evils and troubles befell them. Rather, the face of redemption remains concealed, while they stand within the promise of His merciful countenance: ‘Even so, when they are in their enemies’ land, I have not rejected or abhorred them’—until they add complete confession and complete repentance to that regret.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Ramban addresses the same textual difficulty: why does concealment follow Israel’s recognition of its fault? He distinguishes the continuing delay of redemption from the earlier hiding of mercy; recognition has already changed the relationship. Rav Tzadok offers a different explanation of the concealment: the divine “Anochi” is present within the apparently human innovations of Oral Torah. The comparison marks their different explanations while clarifying why the second concealment need not mean renewed abandonment.

At first there were only twelve log. Consider how much the pot absorbs, how much the roots absorb, and how much the fire consumes. this section with an introduction from here:
"To the man who is good before Him
נָתַן חָכְמָה וָדַעַת וְשִׂמְחָה [קֹהֶלֶת ב, כו]
He gives wisdom, knowledge and joy" (Koheles 2:26) —
"and to the sinner He gives the task
"to give to him who is good before God" (ibid.) —
as it is written (Esther 8:2), "And Esther set
Mordechai over the house of Haman."
And since he made this the opening to the Megillah,
it implies that this is the entire matter
And in truth we must understand
why Hashem Yisbarach brought it about
the house of Haman to Esther;
was there any lack of wealth
to give to Mordechai and Esther?
that regarding the exile of Egypt it is written,
they made it like a deep
like a trap that has no grain
וּבַבִּזָּה לֹא שָׁלְחוּ אֶת יָדָם [אֶסְתֵּר ט, י].
"But on the spoil they did not lay their hand" (Esther 9:10).
and the task was to extract
and many of the eirev rav
"and surname himself by the name of Yisrael."
This is not so with Amalek,
for it is stated in the Mechilta
that they would not accept a convert from Amalek.
and this is what it says:
"But on the spoil they did not lay their hand."
יֵשׁ לְהָבִין מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ עַל הָמָן
we must understand what they said about Haman:
"and to the sinner He gives the task
to give to him who is good," etc. —
But it is as they said
some studied Torah in Bnei Brak";
and in the Ein Yaakov the reading is "converts,"
and they counted Rav Shmuel bar Shilas.
And although we do not accept
it appears that Rav Shmuel bar Shilas
who cohabited with a Jewish woman,
and he came forth from Haman
And see in Sefer Yuchasin, letter shin,
which wrote that the Geonim said
and they counted Rav Shmuel bar Shilas,
and they would not have mixed their family,
who descend from Shimei, the brother of David,
with converts. Until here are his words.
And according to what we have said,
the words of the Geonim work out well.
And this is the matter with Shaul HaMelech,
who was like a year-old child
who had not tasted the taste of sin
and what did he see in this,
דִּכְתִיב [שְׁמוּאֵל א טו, ט] וַיַּחְמֹל שָׁאוּל
that it is written (I Shmuel 15:9), "And Shaul had pity
and because of this there came forth from him
"And what did the Benjamite repay me?
For Shaul did not kill Agag,
from whom Haman was born," etc.
But according to what has been said,
Shaul saw that there was in him,
in Agag, the root of the soul
which had not yet come forth from him;
and about this spark it is written,
And this is the matter of what they said
And in the Ein Yaakov the reading is:
He will make him at peace with you,"
and there it refers to the yetzer hara,
a wicked man to engage in Torah,
so that it may have nourishment
feed him the bread of Torah
and give him to drink the water of Torah,
for in the end He will make him at peace with you,
so that it will not entice you to sin
But here it is not understood
what was intended by the feast
that she made for him, according to this.
And it appears that Esther did not know
in what manner the miracle would come,
that Haman would make peace with her
And according to this we will understand
what they said in the Midrash
this is Esther the queen, etc.;
for Achashverosh and for Haman the wicked, etc.
And the beginning of the passage (ibid. 1) is
of the wisdom of the Torah,
and so it is expounded in the Midrash (there):

to awaken in him, in Haman,
that was in him in concealment,
of the soul of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas;
and this is "she has mixed her wine" —
the wine of the Oral Torah,
along the lines of what they said
and she thought that perhaps through this

it is stated: "The nations of the world

a goodness that is no goodness";
so how does the verse say about Haman,

he went out from Esther's feast
for the moment in which Esther awakened in him
from the soul of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas,
"and he neither rose nor stirred for him,

took vengeance on him and his sons
as they said in the Tikkunei Zohar,
that is, the fifty gates of Binah,
and it later entered into Yisrael.

But the expression "from her father's house"
And according to what was said, it is settled:
since she was of his seed,
and he had pity on Agag,
that is, on account of the spark
of the root of the soul
and she thought that she could
bring Haman back to the good,
and he would make peace with her

of the spreading forth of Torah she'b'al peh,
after they carried out on him and through him
the eradication of Amalek as was fitting.

to the teshuvah that they did.

of the spreading forth of Torah she'b'al peh,

"and to the sinner He gives the task
in which there was the holiness

and he was called by his mother's name

by the name of his mother, the daughter of Shmuel

And this is what it says:
"To the man who is good before Him

and there it speaks of the Written Torah,

"For I have given you a good teaching," etc. (Mishlei 4:2);
and likewise the Torah she'b'al peh
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [תְּהִלִּים קיט, עב] טוֹב לִי
is the Torah of Your mouth," etc. —
that is, the Torah she'b'al peh,
along the lines of what it says (Mishlei 2:6),
"from His mouth come knowledge and understanding"

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [אֶסְתֵּר ח, טז] אוֹרָה וְשִׂמְחָה
Chochmah and Binah, which it is.

through the joining of the wisdom in the mind
with the understanding in the heart;
that is, he merited the drawing down
"And to the sinner He gives the task
that is, the wealth in which
of the soul of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas;
that gives life to the person,
in the secret of "And You give life
(and it was explained in Parshas Shekalim, end of maamar 1;
And this is what they said:
"to give to him who is good before God" —
and it is in line with what they said
and let Mordechai come and take it from him
for the building of the Second Temple;
and this is "to give to him who is good
for in the Second Temple era there were
the Men of the Great Assembly,
and made a fence for the Torah,
and the Chamber of Hewn Stone,
and this is the essence of Torah she'b'al peh,

Mordechai over the house of Haman,"
as we said regarding what they said,
that he is head of all the spices.
that Haman was hanged on a gallows
they were aroused to the spreading forth
and to institute ordinances and fences,
and they instituted days of feasting and gladness,
which is the wine of the Torah
out of love for the miracle,
It turns out, then, that through
the light of Torah she'b'al peh,
after Mordechai and Esther absorbed and gathered,
in which were the holy sparks
from the light of Torah she'b'al peh,
And this is what is alluded to
they merited to root the Torah she'b'al peh,

paragraphs.text: Megillah 15b:12–13 — “The Sages taught: What did Esther see that led her to invite Haman? Rabbi Elazar says: She laid traps for him, as it is written, ‘May their table before them become a trap.’ Rabbi Yehoshua says: She learned from her father’s house, as it is said, ‘If your enemy is hungry, feed him bread.’ Rabbi Meir says: So that he would not form a plan and rebel.” The passage presents several explanations. paragraphs.text: Esther Rabbah 3:11 — “‘When the king’s heart was good with wine’: Rabbi Yitzhak said, Idolaters have no goodness, as it is written, ‘It will not be good for the wicked.’ They objected: But is it not written, ‘When the king’s heart was good with wine’? p: And this is the matter of what they said
and so this psalm is expounded
And they said in the Midrash (there):
This is what the verse says (Yeshayah 10:17):
"And the light of Yisrael shall be for a fire,
and his Holy One for a flame."
"The light of Yisrael" — this is Mordechai;
"and his Holy One for a flame" — this is Esther;
"and it shall burn and devour" — this is Haman —
But it may be said that it is
עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר [עוֹבַדְיָה א, יח]
in line with what it says (Ovadyah 1:18):
"And the house of Yaakov shall be a fire,
and the house of Yosef a flame," etc.
as it says (Devarim 33:2), "From His right hand
And Yosef is the mighty one
the fire of the yetzer hara;
as has been explained many times.
And this is why "the light of Yisrael" is expounded
as it is written, "And Esther set
Mordechai over the house of Haman,"
and he is called "the light of Yisrael"
on account of the Torah she'b'al peh,
that is, the light of Hashem,
and so here it is called "the light of Yisrael":
the light of Torah she'b'al peh,
which is from the side of Yisrael;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [יִרְמְיָה כג, כט] הֲלֹא כֹה
which I have placed in your mouth" (Yeshayah 59:21);
and so they learned from this verse
"And his Holy One for a flame" — this is Esther;
it is in line with what they said
was of the aspect of Yosef HaTzaddik,
along the lines of what they said
And this is what they said in the Gemara
why then was she called Hadassah?
And the tzaddikim are called hadassim
that the myrtle gives a good fragrance;
הַדּוּדָאִים נָתְנוּ רֵיחַ [שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ז, יד]
these are the young men of Yisrael
who have not tasted the taste of sin;
and we have already said many times
that since it used the expression
of the sin of blemishing the bris,
which youth and young manhood bring on
(and it was explained in Rosh Chodesh Marcheshvan, maamar 3);
and a tzaddik, who is a chariot
for the attribute of Yesod Olam,
because he gives a good fragrance;
and since Esther was called Hadassah,
it follows that she was a tzaddekes
and holy, of the aspect of Yosef HaTzaddik.
And this is what they said:
and put a she-demon in her place,
And this is why it expounded
"and his Holy One for a flame — this is Esther":
from the aspect of "the tzaddik is the foundation of the world";
as it says, "and the house of Yosef a flame,"
"And it shall burn and devour" — this is Haman,
who is the root of Amalek,
and then they instituted days of feasting —
the wine of the Oral Torah,
for the heart was made upright,
so that even the heart of the fool, at his left,
"and for the upright in heart, gladness."
And with Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him,
בְּיוֹם הִגָּמֵל אֶת יִצְחָק [בְּרֵאשִׁית כא, ח].
on the day Yitzchak was weaned" (Bereishis 21:8).
the main part of the meal was the drinking.
And this is in line with what they said
was the beginning of the light,
and understood one thing from another,
and therefore on the day of the weaning
of the wine of the Oral Torah.
רַק שָׁם כְּתִיב מִשְׁתֶּה גָּדוֹל שֶׁאָמְרוּ
Only, there it is written "a great feast," for they said
"The Great One of the worlds was there";
which includes all the first three.
just as at the time of Matan Torah,
was included in the Written Torah,
that it is from Hashem Yisbarach,
of Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him,
which is called halachah l'Moshe miSinai
(and it was explained in Chanukah, maamar 2,
the Torah she'b'al peh is in concealment,
in that it seems to the Sages
that they are the ones originating it,
and it is of the aspect of Malchus:
of Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues,
And in truth they too are
the words of the Living God:
"My words which I have placed in your mouth";
and this is the aspect of concealment,
And therefore they expounded from the "great feast"
of Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him,
that Hakadosh Baruch Hu will in the future
make a feast for the tzaddikim
on the day He bestows His kindness
for the essence of the future feast
is the revelation of the secrets of the Torah
and although the Raavad disputed him,
is explicit in the Midrash HaNe'lam
(and it was explained in Terumah, maamar 14);
the wine of the Oral Torah,
that will be in the future,
that it is from Hashem Yisbarach.
so long as a person is in a body.
And this is called a "great feast,"
that the Great One of the worlds is there,
will reveal the secrets to the tzaddikim.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 135b, Toldos, Midrash HaNeelam — “Rabbi Elazar said: In one place we learned that they ‘enjoy,’ and in another that they ‘are nourished.’ What is the difference? His father explained: The righteous who have not merited so much enjoy that radiance, which they do not apprehend so fully; but the righteous who have merited are nourished until they attain complete apprehension. There is no eating and drinking except this; this is the feast and the eating. From where do we know it? From Moshe, of whom it is written that he was there with Hashem for forty days and forty nights; he ate no bread and drank no water, because he was nourished from another feast, from the radiance above. So is the feast of the righteous in the future. ... Rabbi Yosi said: Wine preserved in its grapes from the six days of Creation—these are ancient matters that have not been revealed to a person since the world was created, and that are destined to be revealed to the righteous in the future. This is the drinking and eating; this it certainly is.” The translated excerpt begins after the 135b folio marker in the first preserved record. It explicitly interprets the nourishment and preserved wine through apprehension of divine radiance and previously hidden matters, supporting the comparison Rav Tzadok makes without erasing Raavad’s objection.
